Maladaptive Strategies.value: avoid anything that could cause negative or positive feelings
avoid anything that could be stressful
constantly scan environment for signs of threat

Threat.value: I feel threatened by strangers approaching me even in ordinary situations
I always choose where to sit based on how safe or protected I feel

Memory.value: The memory feels like it belongs to someone else rather than to me
When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event.
When the memory returns I feel physical pain in the same parts of my body as during the event

Negative Appraisals.value: There is something about me that made the event happen
My life has been destroyed by the trauma
What happened to me was deeply unfair and nothing has been done about it

issues.item: Never Alone: make sure never to be alone with another person
issues.explanation: 'Never Alone' is hard to reconcile with the trauma type of police violence and the rest of the profile. This item more strongly suggests fear of being alone with a potentially abusive intimate or familiar person, whereas the threat items center on strangers and general vigilance. That mismatch is difficult to explain clinically within the same trauma-linked profile.

issues.item: Contamination: I feel dirty or contaminated because of what happened
issues.explanation: 'Contamination' is not well aligned with the trauma type and accompanying appraisals. Feeling dirty or contaminated is more characteristic of sexual trauma; with police violence, and with the current memory/threat content, this appraisal stands out as clinically incongruent rather than merely unusual.

vignette: Arthur had never expected the blue lights to find him outside his own home on a Tuesday evening. He had been taking out the recycling when a cruiser turned the corner, tires crunching on gravel. He raised his hands before the engine even cut, but the officers' voices came out clipped and urgent, a synchronized shout that cut through the quiet neighborhood. He felt the sharp bite of the curb against his knee as they forced him down, the heavy weight of a boot on his shoulder, the metallic clack of cuffs clicking shut. He remembered the static hiss of the radio and the sharp, rhythmic commands, words that felt like stones dropping into his chest. He lay there, breathing shallowly, certain he could do nothing but endure until they stood him up and told him to go home. The incident was logged, then quietly shelved. Nothing was filed against him. The case went nowhere. Weeks turned into months, and the reactions to daily life shifted. Arthur noticed he could no longer recall the incident as a story he had lived. When it surfaced, it arrived as if it belonged to another man, the faces and voices blurred at the edges, yet the ache in his right knee and the tightness across his ribs arrived with unmistakable precision. He would sometimes sit at his kitchen table and hear the radio's crackle again, a sharp echo that made his fingers tense around his coffee mug. What frightened him most was the quiet conviction that something about his own posture, his own voice, must have drawn the encounter in the first place. He told himself that if he had stood differently, the night might have ended before it began. He watched the local news with a growing, bitter certainty that the injustice sat unaddressed while he bore the weight alone. He watched his practice hours shrink and his evenings grow hollow, certain that the life he had built had been permanently destroyed. To steady his days, Arthur began steering clear of anything that might stir a reaction. He refused to let himself feel the lift of a good day or the weight of a bad one, keeping his emotions flat to prevent any sudden shift in his pulse. He stopped answering calls after six, declined invitations to dinner, and told his partner he needed to stay home. He began treating any shift in routine as a threat to his stability, restructuring his weeks around predictability. At the clinic, he always parked in the far corner of the lot and walked the perimeter of the building, his eyes moving constantly over the street, the parking garage, the side doors, cataloging every figure that approached the property line. In the operatory, he chose the stool closest to the double doors, angling it so he could watch the hallway and the waiting area without turning his head. When a new patient's spouse leaned over the partition to ask a question, Arthur's shoulders jumped before he could consciously catch himself. He would smile, ask the standard pre-op questions, but his mind remained fixed on the approach, the angle of the door, the distance between the visitor and his chair. For nearly two years he had kept the routine tight, but the quiet had grown too heavy to carry alone. His partner had noticed how he flinched when the phone rang, how he canceled trips before they were even planned, how the practice schedule was unraveling despite the waiting list. Arthur finally sat in the intake room of the community clinic, his hands resting flat on his knees to steady the familiar tremor. He was not sure if the appointment would change anything, but he was tired of waking at 2 a.m. with his heart hammering against his ribs, tired of the phantom echo of commands and the dull, familiar ache in his knee when the television played images of uniformed officers. He wanted to know if he could ever stop bracing for a door to open, if he could sit in a room without calculating his exit, and if the life he had built could somehow be reclaimed from the wreckage he was certain belonged to him now.
